steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper "Cocktail", a pipeline that mixes several control modalities for text-conditional diffusion image generation. Explain why text alone isn't enough, what goes wrong with existing multi-modal control methods, outline the three components of our approach, and finish with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Text-conditional diffusion models and why text-only control falls short
2. Existing approach: modifying the prior
3. Existing approach: hyper-networks injecting control signals, and their problems with multiple modalities
4. Our pipeline, Cocktail, and its three components
5. gControlNet + ControlNorm; spatial guidance sampling
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Text-conditional diffusion models
- high-quality generation; many high-calibre images from short text prompts
- but language hard to capture exact imagery the user wants: ambiguity, subjective interpretation of verbal descriptions
- small prompt changes -> distinct outputs -> no refined control over generation

2. Modifying the prior
- existing solutions for multi-modal control, e.g. control of entire prior space (Fig. 1 (a))
- no localised image modification, no preservation of background
- usually trained from scratch -> lots of resources

3. Hyper-network methods
- following latent-representation methods; extra lightweight hyper-network encodes external control signals into latent vectors, injects them into backbone
- fine for single extra modality, limited for multiple (Fig 1 (b))
- each modality needs its own network -> overhead grows with number of modalities
- additive coefficients between modes matter; imbalance among superimposed modes -> coefficients pivotal for output
- sampling: initial inference without control signal injection -> object placement may contradict control signals

4. Cocktail (Fig. 1 (c))
- multi-modality control through a text-conditional diffusion model
- three components: 1) hyper-network accepting multi-modal input, 2) conditional normalisation to mix control features, 3) sampling strategy for precise control
- Fig. 2: images meeting all conditions or any subset, one single model

5. Components in more detail
- gControlNet: branched network, accepts multiple modalities; after training takes arbitrary combinations; fuses modalities in the same region automatically, balances disparities
- ControlNorm (controllable normalisation): uses gControlNet features; decoupling -> better semantic and spatial representation of control signals
- spatial guidance sampling: distinct prompts separate entities from background; entities put into background via prompt editing; avoids undesired entities

6. Contributions
- Generalized ControlNet (gControlNet): adaptive multi-modal integration, handles imbalance between modalities
- Controllable Normalisation (ControlNorm): better use of information in branched networks
- spatial guidance sampling via attention map operations: region-specific generation, no undesired objects outside specified regions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Text-conditional diffusion models now make high-quality generation possible. With these models you can generate lots of high-quality images just by using short text prompts. But it is hard for language to describe exactly the image that the user has in mind, because verbal descriptions can be ambiguous and are interpreted subjectively when it comes to visual synthesis. Also, if the text prompt is changed only a little, the output image also comes out different, which shows that there is no refined control over the generation process.

One group of existing solutions for multi-modal control is to modify the prior, for example controlling the whole prior space, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Because these approaches work on the whole prior, they cannot do local modifications to an image and they cannot keep the background elements. Also, these models usually need to be trained from scratch, and that needs a lot of resources.

In response to the methods that work with latent representation, an extra lightweight hyper-network is introduced in other recent work, which encodes external control signals into latent vectors and then injects them directly into the backbone network. These methods handle control from a single additional modality well, but they have limitations when there are multiple modalities, as shown in Fig 1 (b). One issue is that every modality needs its own network, so the computational overhead grows proportionally as the number of modalities grows. Another thing to consider is the additive coefficients between different modes and how they affect the final images. Since the superimposed modes are imbalanced, these additive coefficients become a key factor for the final synthesized output. There is one more challenge in the sampling process, when the model first does an initial inference with no control signal injected. This first inference step can place objects in a way that may contradict the control signals.

4. Cocktail (Fig. 1 (c))
- multi-modality control through a text-conditional diffusion model
- three components: hyper-network for multi-modal input; conditional normalisation to mix control features; sampling strategy for precise control
- Fig. 2: all conditions or any subset, one single model

5. Components
- gControlNet: branched, multiple modalities, arbitrary combinations after training, fuses modalities in same region and balances them
- ControlNorm: uses gControlNet features, decoupling -> better semantic/spatial representation
- spatial guidance sampling: distinct prompts for entities vs background, prompt editing, avoids undesired entities

6. Contributions
- gControlNet; ControlNorm; spatial guidance sampling (attention map, no undesired objects outside regions)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Text-conditional diffusion models now make high-quality generation possible. With these models you can generate lots of high-quality images just by using short text prompts. But it is hard for language to describe exactly the image that the user has in mind, because verbal descriptions can be ambiguous and are interpreted subjectively when it comes to visual synthesis. Also, if the text prompt is changed only a little, the output image also comes out different, which shows that there is no refined control over the generation process.

One group of existing solutions for multi-modal control is to modify the prior, for example controlling the whole prior space, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Because these approaches work on the whole prior, they cannot do local modifications to an image and they cannot keep the background elements. Also, these models usually need to be trained from scratch, and that needs a lot of resources.

In response to the methods that work with latent representation, an extra lightweight hyper-network is introduced in other recent work, which encodes external control signals into latent vectors and then injects them directly into the backbone network. These methods handle control from a single additional modality well, but they have limitations when there are multiple modalities, as shown in Fig 1 (b). One issue is that every modality needs its own network, so the computational overhead grows proportionally as the number of modalities grows. Another thing to consider is the additive coefficients between different modes and how they affect the final images. Since the superimposed modes are imbalanced, these additive coefficients become a key factor for the final synthesized output. There is one more challenge in the sampling process, when the model first does an initial inference with no control signal injected. This first inference step can place objects in a way that may contradict the control signals.

In this paper, we propose a new pipeline called Cocktail, shown in Fig. 1 (c), which does multi-modality control through a text-conditional diffusion model. It has three main components: 1) a hyper-network that can take multi-modal input, 2) a conditional normalisation method to mix the control features, and 3) a sampling strategy for precise control over the generation process. As Fig. 2 shows, our method can generate images that meet all the input conditions or any subset of them, using only one single model.

To do this, we first trained a branched network called gControlNet that accepts multiple modalities. After training, the branched network can accept any combination of the existing modalities at the same time. When multiple modalities are in the same region, the model can automatically fuse the input from the different modalities and balance the differences between them. To make use of the features of gControlNet, we also proposed controllable normalisation (ControlNorm). Because of the decoupling that ControlNorm gives, we can represent the control signals better in semantic and spatial terms.

We also introduce a spatial guidance sampling method so that spatial generation can be done under multi-modal control signals. Specifically, we use different textual prompts to tell entities apart from the background, and the entities are put into the background with a prompt editing approach. This sampling approach is effective at avoiding the generation of entities we don't want.

Our main contributions are as follows:

- We introduced the Generalized ControlNet (gControlNet), a branched network that can adaptively integrate multi-modal information, which deals with the issues that come from imbalances between modalities;

- We proposed the Controllable Normalisation (ControlNorm) to make better use of the information in branched networks and get more effective outcomes;

- We introduced a spatial guidance sampling method based on operations in the attention map, to generate the relevant information for regional contexts and avoid including undesired objects outside the specified regions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Text-conditional diffusion models [1,2,3,4] have made high-quality generation possible. These models allow an array of high-calibre images to be generated from concise textual prompts. However, language has inherent difficulty in capturing exactly the imagery the user expects, owing to the ambiguities and subjective interpretations of verbal descriptions in the context of visual synthesis. Moreover, minor changes to the textual prompts yield distinct visual outputs, which underscores the absence of refined control over the generative process.

Modifying the prior is one line of existing solutions for multi-modal control, e.g., control of the entire prior space [2,5,6,7,8] as demonstrated in Fig. 1 (a). Since these approaches are centered on the whole prior, they lack the capacity for localised image modifications and for preserving background elements. Moreover, these models typically have to be trained from scratch, which demands substantial resources.

In response to the methods dealing with latent representation [9,10,11], an additional lightweight hyper-network is introduced in [12,13] to encode external control signals into latent vectors and inject them directly into the backbone network. Such methods handle control over a single additional modality effectively, but they show limitations when confronted with multiple modalities, as shown in Fig 1 (b). One issue is that each modality requires its own network, so the computational overhead escalates proportionally with the number of modalities. Furthermore, the impact of additive coefficients between different modes on the final imaging outcome needs to be considered: the inherent imbalance among superimposed modes makes these coefficients a pivotal factor in the synthesized output. An additional challenge arises during sampling, when the model conducts an initial inference without control signal injection. This preliminary step can lead to object placement that contradicts the control signals.

In this paper, we propose a novel pipeline termed Cocktail, shown in Fig. 1 (c), which accomplishes multi-modality control through a text-conditional diffusion model. It consists of three main components: 1) a hyper-network capable of accommodating multi-modal input, 2) a conditional normalisation method to mix the control features, and 3) a sampling strategy designed for precise control over the generative process. As shown in Fig. 2, our method can generate images that meet all input conditions or any arbitrary subset of them, using only one single model.

To achieve this, we first trained a branched network named gControlNet that accepts multiple modalities. Once trained, the branched network can simultaneously accept arbitrary combinations of existing modalities. When multiple modalities coexist in the same region, the model automatically fuses the input from different modalities and balances the disparities between them. To leverage the features of gControlNet, we further proposed controllable normalisation (ControlNorm). Thanks to the decoupling provided by ControlNorm, we can achieve a better representation of control signals in both semantic and spatial aspects.

Moreover, we introduce a spatial guidance sampling method to facilitate spatial generation under multi-modal control signals. Specifically, we use distinct textual prompts to differentiate entities from the background and incorporate the entities into the background via prompt editing. This sampling approach is effective in avoiding the generation of undesired entities.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

- We introduced the Generalized ControlNet (gControlNet), a branched network capable of adaptively integrating multi-modal information, which addresses issues stemming from imbalances between modalities;

- We proposed the Controllable Normalisation (ControlNorm) to optimize the use of information within branched networks and yield more effective outcomes;

- We introduced a spatial guidance sampling method based on operations within the attention map to generate information tailored to regional contexts, preventing undesired objects from appearing outside the specified regions.
